opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because as a company scales, the default is that culture dilutes. When you're fifty people, everyone can hear directly from the founders. Everyone knows why decisions are made. When you're several thousand people, there are layers, and every layer is a chance for the message to get distorted, like a game of telephone.

So one of the things I try to do is talk to the whole company directly and pretty regularly. I write fairly long internal documents, and we have sessions where I'll just get up and talk about what I'm thinking: where I think the technology is going, what I'm worried about, what the strategic picture looks like, and why we're making the trade-offs we're making. And I try to be very unfiltered about it. I don't want it to sound like corporate communications. I'd rather say "here's something I'm uncertain about" or "here's a decision I think we might have gotten wrong" than present a polished, sanitized version.

The reason that matters is that the mission only works if people actually understand it, not just the slogan. If people just hear "we care about safety," that's not very useful. What's useful is understanding the reasoning: why we think it's important to be at the frontier, what tensions that creates, and where the lines are that we won't cross. If people understand the reasoning, they can make good decisions in situations I'll never see. That's the only way it scales. I can't be in every room.

There's also a trust element. If people hear things directly from me, including the uncomfortable things, they're less likely to feel like there's a hidden agenda. And when there's a hard decision, or when the outside world is saying something about us, people already have context. They're not learning about it from Twitter.

I don't want to overstate it. My talking isn't what makes the culture. The culture is really the thousands of people who choose to work here and hold each other to the standard. But I think the leader's job is partly to keep articulating what the standard is, over and over, even when it feels repetitive. It's a bit like a lighthouse: it's not doing the sailing, but it helps everyone know where they are.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders must repeatedly articulate the company’s mission, reasoning, and standards so employees understand the purpose and can make decisions that sustain the culture.

r002.rationale: It describes growth from 50 people to several thousand and says the speaker talks to the whole company about the technology, strategy, and trade-offs, beyond individual conversations.

r003.rationale: It explains that direct communication avoids message distortion through layers of management and gives employees context that the speaker cannot provide in every room.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, actually. When you're thirty or fifty people, culture just kind of happens by osmosis. Everyone's in the same room, everyone knows why we started the company, everyone has heard me ramble about why I think this technology is dangerous and also why I think it's enormously important. You don't have to do anything deliberate. But once you're past a few hundred people, and certainly past a thousand, that stops working. Most people at the company have never had a long conversation with me, and the thing that originally animated the founders becomes a kind of telephone game. It gets transmitted through managers, through onboarding docs, through whatever the loudest person on Slack happens to think the mission is.

And I found that the telephone game degrades in a particular way. It's not that people get the facts wrong, it's that they lose the reasoning. They end up with the conclusions without the arguments. So someone might know "Anthropic is a safety-focused lab," but if they don't understand why we think the stakes are what they are, or why we chose to build frontier models rather than just do research on the sidelines, then the culture becomes a set of slogans. And slogans are brittle. The first time there's real commercial pressure, or a competitor ships something, a slogan doesn't hold. An argument you actually understand does.

So that's why I think direct communication matters more than most CEOs probably assume. I do these long written things, I do these all-hands where I try to lay out my actual thinking, including the parts where I'm uncertain or where I think we've made mistakes. I'm not very good at the short, punchy, inspirational version anyway, so I'd rather just give people the full argument and let them stress-test it. And honestly a lot of the value is that people push back. If a thousand people hear my reasoning directly, some of them are going to find the holes, and I'd much rather find those out from inside the company than from the world.

The other piece is that it sets the norm that this is how we talk here. If the CEO explains the "why" at length and is willing to say "I don't know" or "here's where I'm worried we're wrong," then it's much harder for a middle manager to run their team on vibes and authority. It's not that I'm trying to be the single source of culture, that would actually be unhealthy and wouldn't scale either. It's more that I'm trying to keep the signal clean enough that it can propagate through all those other layers without turning into mush.

I'll say the honest caveat, which is that I don't know how long this works. There's probably some size where even very direct, very frequent communication from one person just isn't enough, and you need the culture to be fully carried by the institutions and the people you hired. We're trying to build that too. But at least for now, I think the cheapest, highest-leverage thing I can do is make sure people are hearing the actual reasoning, from me, in my own words, rather than a summary of a summary.

r001.rationale: The response says direct communication shares the founders’ purpose and the reasoning behind Anthropic’s safety focus, helping keep its culture from becoming slogans.

r002.rationale: It says communication stops working by osmosis once the company passes a few hundred or a thousand people, but does not identify roughly 2,500 employees.

r003.rationale: It describes how the founding rationale gets degraded as it passes through managers and other layers, and says direct communication lets employees hear the reasoning from the CEO.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of culture is people understanding how you make decisions, not just hearing a list of values. You can say, “We care about safety, we care about being honest,” but the hard part is what those things mean when there’s a real tradeoff. Does someone feel comfortable bringing you bad news? Can they challenge an assumption behind something the company is doing?

As you grow, fewer people get to see those decisions happen firsthand. So direct communication helps make the reasoning visible. Here’s what we’re trying to accomplish, here’s why we made this choice, here’s what we’re uncertain about. And people need a chance to ask questions, including uncomfortable questions.

But it only works if what I say matches what people experience. If I encourage disagreement and then react badly when someone disagrees, that reaction communicates much more than anything I said. So I think direct communication is useful for sustaining culture, but ultimately the culture comes from how we behave.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses making decisions and values explicit, but does not identify leaders’ articulation of Anthropic’s purpose as a way to sustain culture.

r002.rationale: It says fewer people witness decisions firsthand as the company grows, but gives no roughly 2,500-employee scale or explains the need to communicate direction company-wide beyond individual conversations.

r003.rationale: The candidate supports direct communication and opportunities for questions, but does not state that it creates a connection difficult to achieve through management layers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of culture is about explaining why we’re doing things, and doing that repeatedly. When you’re a small company, people pick it up from being in the room with you. As you grow, you can’t rely on that happening automatically.

So I try to talk directly to people about what I’m thinking, what I’m worried about, and how particular decisions connect to the mission. If all people hear is the decision, they can follow that decision, but they don’t necessarily have the context to make the next one themselves.

And it has to go both ways. People need to be able to ask hard questions and say, “This doesn’t seem consistent with what you said before.” That’s useful feedback. The goal isn’t to have everyone repeat the same words. It’s to have enough shared understanding that people can exercise good judgment without everything going through me.

r001.rationale: The response says leaders should repeatedly explain why the company is doing things and how decisions connect to its mission, identifying purpose articulation as a way to sustain culture.

r002.rationale: It says that growth makes informal learning insufficient, but it does not mention roughly 2,500 employees or explain the need for company-wide communication beyond individual conversations.

r003.rationale: The response advocates direct communication and says shared understanding helps people act without everything going through the speaker, but it does not say that direct contact provides a connection difficult to achieve through management layers.
